newsitem.title: USA: Orange County grand jurors tell of Merrill probe.
newsitem.headline: Orange County grand jurors tell of Merrill probe.

text.p: Two members of the grand jury that investigated Merrill Lynch & Co's role in the Orange County bankruptcy crisis said criminal charges would have been difficult to prove had they been brought, according to a published report on Wednesday.
The former grand jurors also told the Los Angeles Times that the panel might not have returned indictments even if Orange County prosecutors had sought them.
"Assuming the district attorney could have gotten an indictment, it would have been a very difficult, very complicated case," said Donald Wecker, the grand jury foreman.

The southern California county shocked Wall Street in December 1994 when it filed for bankruptcy after losing more than $1.6 billion on risky investments. The county emerged from bankruptcy one year ago.

In June, Merrill Lynch settled with Orange County District Attorney Michael Capizzi. The controversial $30 million settlement ensured that Merrill Lynch and its employees would not face criminal charges from county prosecutors.

Initially, Capizzi said county prosecutors would try to unseal transcripts from the grand jury's investigation. But prosecutors later announced that they could not release the files because no indictments were issued.
Earlier this week, lawyers for the county asked a Superior Court judge to give them access to the transcripts for use in the county's $2 billion-plus civil lawsuit against the brokerage giant.
The two grand jurors interviewed by the Los Angeles Times urged county prosecutors to make the transcripts public.
"Since we never got into discussions (about an indictment) I don't think there's anything really confidential," grand juror Henry Legere told the Times.
